facts.quote: The building includes exhibition spaces, workshops, a library, an auditorium with 150 seats, and a café.

facts.fact: The first scheme, shown to the city in 2008, was rejected as too tall; only the third attempt was accepted, in December 2012.
facts.quote: The first project for LUMA Arles was presented by Maja Hoffmann and Frank Gehry in July 2008 to the city of Arles. It was rejected for being too tall. Only the third attempt was accepted in December 2012.

facts.fact: The arts centre also includes several renovated former railway workshops.
facts.quote: It encompasses several renovated former railroad factories and the LUMA Tower, a 15,000 square meter tower building designed by the Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry for the LUMA Foundation.

facts.fact: The museum in Menton is devoted to Jean Cocteau and holds the collection of Séverin Wunderman.
facts.quote: The Jean Cocteau Museum/Séverin Wunderman Collection is a museum in Menton, on the French Riviera, in the Alpes-Maritimes department. Dedicated to the French artist Jean Cocteau, it incorporates the collection of American businessman and Cocteau enthusiast Séverin Wunderman.

facts.fact: The city held an international design competition in 2007; the winner was announced in June 2008 and the shell was finished in January 2011.
facts.quote: An international competition was held by the council in 2007, with a winner for the design of the museum announced in June 2008. The foundation stone was laid in December 2008, with the shell completed in January 2011.

facts.fact: The competition was won by French architect Rudy Ricciotti.
facts.quote: The competition to design the museum building was won by French architect Rudy Ricciotti, an exponent of 'hedonist architecture' in the 1980s.

facts.fact: Ricciotti based the design on Cocteau's life and work, using black and white as an interplay of structural forces recalling the artist's works on paper.
facts.quote: Ricciotti's design was directly inspired by Cocteau's life and work, he has said of the museum's design that "Black and white no longer serve as colours here...they create an interplay of structural forces calling to mind both the artist’s works on paper and the poet’s personality, his zones of light and darkness, his enigmatic self-mythology fueled by contrasts."

facts.fact: Its façade of jagged black pillars has been compared to a set of teeth and to a spider.
facts.quote: The distinctive facade of the building has been variously described as "...like a fierce set of teeth or a string of alabaster forearms holding up the sky" and "...like a spider, with jagged black pillars sprawling leg-like over the building".

facts.fact: The museum took eight years to create and covers 29,000 sq ft.
facts.quote: The museum took eight years to create, and is 29,000 sq ft in size.

facts.fact: It holds almost 1,000 graphic works by Cocteau, most from Wunderman's collection.
facts.quote: Divided into seven parts, the museum contains almost 1000 graphic works by Cocteau, with the majority of the collection from collector Severin Wunderman.

facts.fact: The museum opened in 2011.
facts.quote: Wunderman donated his collection of almost 1,000 works by the artist to the town of Menton in 2005, and the Musée Jean Cocteau—collection Séverin Wunderman, housed in a building designed by Rudy Ricciotti, opened there in 2011.

facts.fact: OMA designed Villa Dall'Ava between 1984 and 1991, arguably its most mature design up to then.
facts.quote: The second – arguably the most full-grown design of OMA until that date – was Villa Dall'Ava in Paris (1984–1991).

facts.fact: According to Koolhaas, the client asked for a "masterpiece".
facts.quote: The client, according to Koolhaas, asked for a "masterpiece".

facts.fact: The husband wanted a glass house and the wife wanted a swimming pool on the roof.
facts.quote: He wanted a glass house. She wanted a swimming pool on the roof.

facts.fact: Delays dragged on so long that the house became, for OMA, a record of the office growing up.
facts.quote: So many delays plagued the house that it "became a record of our own (OMA's) growing up".

facts.fact: The Pavillon Noir is a choreographic centre in Aix-en-Provence.
facts.quote: The Pavillon Noir is a choreographic center in Aix-en-Provence, France.

facts.fact: It was built as the main rehearsal and performance centre of Ballet Preljocaj, Angelin Preljocaj's dance company.
facts.quote: It was built especially to be the main rehearsal and performance center of the Ballet Preljocaj, a dance company choreographed by Angelin Preljocaj.

facts.fact: Rudy Ricciotti designed it; building began in 2004 and finished in 2006.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Algerian-born French architect Rudy Ricciotti. Its construction began in 2004 and it was completed in 2006.

facts.fact: It is built of steel and concrete.
facts.quote: It is made of steel and concrete.

facts.fact: It has four rehearsal studios and a 378-seat performance hall.
facts.quote: According to its officially website, it has "four rehearsal studios and one performance hall with 378 seats."

facts.fact: It stands at 530 avenue Mozart, near the Bibliothèque Méjanes.
facts.quote: The Pavillon Noir is located at 530 avenue Mozart in Aix-en-Provence. It is near the Bibliothèque Méjanes.

facts.fact: Le Havre's House of Culture was built in 1982 by Oscar Niemeyer and is nicknamed "the Volcano" for its shape.
facts.quote: Another notable architectural work of the central city is that of the House of Culture built in 1982 by the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer and nicknamed "the Volcano" because of the shape of the building.

facts.fact: From 2012 it was refurbished inside and out, with changes approved by Niemeyer, including opening the plaza more to its surroundings.
facts.quote: From 2012, this place was refurbished both inside and outside with fairly significant changes approved by the architect including greater openness to the outside of the plaza.

facts.fact: UNESCO listed the rebuilt city of Le Havre as a World Heritage Site on 15 July 2005.
facts.quote: In commending the reconstruction work UNESCO listed the city of Le Havre on 15 July 2005 as a World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: Upper Lawn Pavilion, on the Fonthill Estate at Tisbury, Wiltshire, was built in 1959–62 and was once the Smithsons' own home.
facts.quote: Upper Lawn Pavilion, Fonthill Estate, Tisbury, Wiltshire (1959–62, once the Smithsons' home).

facts.fact: The Smithsons used it as an experimental building to try out materials, decorative elements and small design changes.
facts.quote: This was utilized by the Smithsons as an experimental building where they could explore different applications of materials, decorative elements, and other small design adjustments that had not yet been widely adopted in the London area.

facts.fact: The house in Hampstead, a lightweight steel structure with glass façades, was one of the first buildings of the practice Michael and Patty Hopkins set up in 1976.
facts.quote: In 1976, Hopkins set up what became Hopkins Architects in partnership with his wife, who had run her own practice. One of their first buildings was their own house in Hampstead, a lightweight steel structure with glass façades.

facts.fact: The Hopkinses' three children grew up in the open-plan house, though they later asked for walls around their bedrooms.
facts.quote: Patty and Michael's three children, Sarah, Abigail and Joel, grew up in the Hopkins’ open-plan house in Hampstead, though the children later demanded that their bedrooms were given walls.

facts.fact: Michael and Patty Hopkins were, with Foster, Rogers, Farrell and Grimshaw, leading figures in bringing high-tech architecture to Britain.
facts.quote: With Foster, Richard Rogers, Terry Farrell and Nicholas Grimshaw, both Hopkins and his wife were leading figures in the introduction of high-tech architecture into Britain.

facts.fact: The memorial marks the killing of 335 civilians and political prisoners by German occupation troops in Rome on 24 March 1944, in reprisal for the Via Rasella attack.
facts.quote: The Ardeatine massacre, or Fosse Ardeatine massacre (Italian: Eccidio delle Fosse Ardeatine), was a mass killing of 335 civilians and political prisoners carried out in Rome on 24 March 1944 by German occupation troops during the Second World War as a reprisal for the Via Rasella attack in central Rome against the SS Police Regiment Bozen the previous day.

facts.fact: The Ardeatine Caves site was declared a Memorial Cemetery and National Monument, open daily to visitors.
facts.quote: Subsequently, the Ardeatine Caves site (Fosse Ardeatine) was declared a Memorial Cemetery and National Monument open daily to visitors.

facts.fact: The design came from a national competition and was a collaboration of five architects (Aprile, Calcaprina, Cardelli, Fiorentino and Perugini) and two sculptors.
facts.quote: The design of the Fosse Ardeatine monument resulted from a national competition and was a collaboration between five architects (Nello Aprile, Cino Calcaprina, Aldo Cardelli, Mario Fiorentino & Giuseppe Perugini) and two sculptors (Francesco Coccia & Mirko Basaldella).

facts.fact: Mirko Basaldella's massive bronze gate draws on the barbed wire of battlefields and camps, merged with the curls of a Tree of Life.
facts.quote: The massive bronze gate by Mirko Basaldella used the ubiquitous barbed wire of battlefields and concentration camps as inspiration, merging it with the moving curlicues of a Tree of Life.

facts.fact: At the entrance stands a colossal concrete statue by Francesco Coccia of three male figures standing together as one.
facts.quote: Also at the entrance is a colossal concrete statue by Francesco Coccia of three male figures standing together as one.

facts.fact: Each face of the statue looks toward a key part of the memorial: the burial slab, the old quarries and the forecourt.
facts.quote: Each face on the statue directs its gaze towards an important element of the memorial complex: the burial slab, the old quarries, and the forecourt.

facts.fact: A state commemoration is held at the monument every year on the anniversary, with the 335 names read out.
facts.quote: Every year, on the anniversary of the slaughter and in the presence of the senior officials of the Italian Republic, a solemn state commemoration is held at the monument in honour of the fallen. Each year, 335 names are called out, a simple roll call of the dead.

facts.fact: The bridge in Potenza links the motorway exit to the main roads into the south of the city.
facts.quote: The "Viadotto dell'Industria" (Industry viaduct), also known as "Bridge over the Basento" river or Musmeci Bridge, is a bridge in Potenza, Basilicata, Italy, that connects the Potenza city center exit on the Sicignano-Potenza motorway with the main access roads in the southern part of the city.

facts.fact: Engineer Sergio Musmeci designed it in 1967 and it was built between 1971 and 1976, embodying his architectural theories.
facts.quote: Designed by the Italian engineer Sergio Musmeci in 1967, and built between 1971 and 1976, the bridge perfectly incarnates Musmeci's architectural theories.

facts.fact: It is a single membrane of reinforced concrete, about 30 cm thick, moulded into four contiguous arches.
facts.quote: The structure's uniqueness is due to its construction: it is made of only one membrane of reinforced concrete (about 30 cm (1 ft) thick) molded to form four contiguous arches.

facts.fact: The concrete sheet forms a finger-like structure that carries the whole bridge and also serves as a footpath.
facts.quote: The concrete sheet is shaped into a "finger-like" structure, which supports the whole bridge, and it is also used as a pedestrian walkway.

facts.fact: It was built without prefabricated elements.
facts.quote: The bridge was built without using prefabricated elements.

facts.fact: In 2003 it was declared a monument of cultural interest by the Ministry of Heritage and Culture.
facts.quote: In 2003, the bridge was declared a "monument of cultural interest" by the Ministry of Heritage and Culture.

facts.fact: The bridge is a motorway viaduct in Genoa over the Polcevera river, designed by Renzo Piano.
facts.quote: The Genoa Saint George Bridge (Italian: Viadotto Genova-San Giorgio) is a motorway viaduct that crosses the Polcevera river and the districts of Sampierdarena and Cornigliano, in the city of Genoa. It was designed by architect Renzo Piano.

facts.fact: It replaces the Ponte Morandi, which partly collapsed on 14 August 2018 and was demolished in June 2019.
facts.quote: The bridge replaces the Ponte Morandi (Polcevera Viaduct), which  partially collapsed on 14 August 2018 and was demolished in June 2019.

facts.fact: It is a mixed steel-and-concrete structure 1,067 m long, with 19 spans on 18 elliptical reinforced-concrete piers.
facts.quote: Built as a mixed steel-concrete structure, it is 1,067 metres (3,501 ft) long, approximately 31 metres (102 ft) wide and 45 metres (148 ft) high and consists of 19 spans supported by 18 elliptical section reinforced concrete stacks with a constant shape.

facts.fact: Robots inspect the underside and clean the wind barriers and solar panels.
facts.quote: The role of these robots was to automate inspection of the lower surface of the bridge and the cleaning of windproof barriers and solar panels.

facts.fact: A system of 240 fibre-optic sensors monitors the deck and piers in real time.
facts.quote: The system is made up of 240 fibre optic sensors and constantly detects the movements of the deck, the inclinations of the piles, the vibrations of the structure and the vehicular traffic, providing real-time reports to the manager of the motorway section.

facts.fact: A dehumidification system limits corrosion from salty condensation.
facts.quote: It also has a dehumidification system to prevent the build-up of saline condensation and limit corrosion damage.

facts.fact: The new bridge opened on 3 August 2020.
facts.quote: The new bridge was inaugurated on 3 August 2020.

facts.fact: The museum in Thessaloniki opened in 1994.
facts.quote: The Museum of Byzantine Culture (Greek: Μουσείο Βυζαντινού Πολιτισμού) is a museum in Thessaloniki, Central Macedonia, Greece, which opened in 1994.

facts.fact: Kyriakos Krokos won a nationwide architectural competition for the museum, announced in 1977.
facts.quote: To design the museum, a nationwide architectural competition was announced in 1977. The competition was ultimately won by the entry of Kyriakos Krokos.

facts.fact: Construction ran from March 1989 to October 1993.
facts.quote: Construction of the building began in March 1989, and was completed in October 1993.

facts.fact: About 1,200 m² of the building is storage, modelled on industrial warehouses.
facts.quote: Approximately 1200 m2 of the building is used as storage space. Industrial warehouses served as a model.

facts.fact: In 2005 it won the Council of Europe's Museum Prize.
facts.quote: In 2005, the museum was awarded the Council of Europe's Museum Prize.

facts.fact: The museum has run educational programmes for schoolchildren since 1998.
facts.quote: Beginning in 1998, the museum has run educational programmes for schoolchildren.

facts.fact: Aris Konstantinidis built the emblematic Weekend House in Anavyssos in 1962, as one of his private projects.
facts.quote: At the same time, Konstantinidis planned and realised several private projects such as the emblematic Weekend House in Anavyssos (1962).

facts.fact: In the 1980s historians including Kenneth Frampton linked Konstantinidis's work to critical regionalism.
facts.quote: In the 1980s, his work was associated with the theory of critical regionalism by renowned architectural historians and theorists Alexander Tzonis & Liane Lefaivre and Kenneth Frampton.

facts.fact: Silver Hut (1984) was one of Toyo Ito's most remarkable early conceptual projects.
facts.quote: His most remarkable early conceptual contributions were made through projects of this scale, such as White U (1976) and Silver Hut (1984).

facts.fact: The original Silver Hut was Ito's own house, next to White U.
facts.quote: 1984 – Silver Hut (Ito's own house, adjacent to White U)

facts.fact: Silver Hut won the Architectural Institute of Japan Award in 1986.
facts.quote: 1986 – Architectural Institute of Japan Award for Silver Hut

facts.fact: At the Toyo Ito Museum of Architecture in Imabari, Silver Hut is one of two small museum buildings, with Steel Hut, on a promontory on the island of Ōmishima in the Seto Inland Sea.
facts.quote: The two small museum buildings, named Steel Hut and Silver Hut, both designed by Pritzker Prize winning architect Toyo Ito, are located on a promontory on Ōmishima, a small island in the middle of the Seto Inland Sea.

facts.fact: The museum opened in 2011 and shows Ito's work and other Japanese contemporary architecture.
facts.quote: Opened in 2011, the museum hosts exhibits and educational programs relating both to the work of Toyo Ito, regional development and other themes in Japanese contemporary architecture.

facts.fact: The Roof House is a project of Tezuka Architects, founded in 1994 by Takaharu and Yui Tezuka.
facts.quote: In 1994, he and his wife Yui Tezuka founded the Tokyo-based firm Tezuka Architects. Projects by Tezuka Architects include the Roof House,  Echigo-Matsunoyama Museum of Natural Science, Fuji Kindergarten and Woods of Net.

facts.fact: The Roof House won the Japan Institute of Architects Prize in 2002.
facts.quote: 2002 – Japan Institute of Architects Prize (Roof House)

facts.fact: It is the main stadium built for the 1986 Asian Games and the 1988 Summer Olympics, and the largest stadium in South Korea.
facts.quote: It is the main stadium built for the 1988 Summer Olympics and the 10th Asian Games in 1986. It is the centrepiece of the Seoul Sports Complex in the Songpa District, in the southeast of the city south of the Han River. It is the largest stadium in South Korea.

facts.fact: Kim Swoo-geun designed it, with a profile that imitates the curves of Joseon white porcelain.
facts.quote: This multi-purpose stadium was designed by Kim Swoo-geun. The lines of the stadium's profile imitate the elegant curves of a Joseon white porcelain.

facts.fact: Seats on two tiers sit under a partly covered roof, for 69,950 spectators.
facts.quote: Spectator seats are distributed across two tiers beneath a partially covered roof structure; seating capacity is 69,950.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1977 for the 1986 Asian Games; it became the Olympic centrepiece when Seoul won the 1988 Games in 1981.
facts.quote: Construction on the new stadium began in 1977 with the aim of staging the Asian Games in 1986. When Seoul was awarded the Games of the XXIV Olympiad in September 1981, this stadium became the centrepiece.

facts.fact: It opened officially on 29 September 1984.
facts.quote: Officially, the stadium opened on 29 September 1984 as the main work for the 10th Asian Games held two years later, then the Olympics in 1988.

facts.fact: It hosted the opening and closing ceremonies, athletics and the football final of the 1988 Olympics.
facts.quote: The events hosted by the stadium during the Olympics were the opening and closing ceremonies, athletics, the football finals, and the equestrian jumping individual final.

facts.fact: Kim Swoo-geun's major works, including the Olympic stadium, combine his view of architecture with Korean traditional elements.
facts.quote: His representative works include "SPACE Group building" (공간 사옥, 1978), "Masan Yangdeok Catholic Church" (마산양덕성당 1979), "Jinju National Museum" (진주국립박물관 1986) and "Olympic Main Stadium" (올림픽 경기장 1987), which feature his characteristic view of architecture as well as Korean traditional elements.

facts.fact: The building stands in Taepyeongno, at the heart of Seoul, with the old city hall (now Seoul Metropolitan Library) and Seoul Plaza in front.
facts.quote: It is located in Taepyeongno, Jung District, at the heart of Seoul. It is connected to City Hall Station  on Seoul Subway Line 1, with access to Seoul Subway Line 2 from the same station. In front of the current city hall is the old city hall building, now Seoul Metropolitan Library, and Seoul Plaza.

facts.fact: Yoo Kerl of iArc won the competition for the new city hall in February 2008.
facts.quote: Following a competition for a new city hall, the jury awarded the commission to Yoo Kerl of iArc on February 18, 2008.

facts.fact: The design draws in part on the eaves of traditional Korean houses.
facts.quote: The design was based in part on the eaves of traditional Korean houses.

facts.fact: It has a double-skin façade and gets over 25 percent of its energy from photovoltaic, solar thermal and geothermal sources.
facts.quote: The building is also designed to be eco-friendly with a double skin facade system and over 25 percent of the energy used in the building from photovoltaic, solar thermal and geothermal sources.

facts.fact: It opened to the public on 27 August 2012 after four years and five months of work.
facts.quote: In 2012, the new City Hall was opened to the public on 27 August and the city government moved in on 1 September. The project, which took four years and five months to complete, also includes multipurpose halls and cultural facilities for citizens.

facts.fact: The old building, a registered cultural asset, became a library.
facts.quote: The old building, registered as a cultural asset, has been converted into a library, and boasts a collection of more than 200,000 books.

facts.fact: Its indoor Green Wall, with over 70,000 plants of 14 species, was named the world's largest vertical garden by Guinness World Records in 2013.
facts.quote: One prominent feature of the Seoul City Hall building is its internal Green Wall, which is an vertical garden wall with over 70,000 plants of 14 different species. The Green Wall spans an area of 1516 square meters and was named in the Guinness World Records as the largest vertical garden in the world in 2013.
